source.title: Double Descent and Malign Overfitting in Diffusion Models
source.authors: Raphaël Urfin; Tony Bonnaire; Giulio Biroli; Marc Mézard

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model size and training time and measures test loss, directly testing descent patterns in a new diffusion-model setting. It also varies noise realizations and regularization.
record.gate_note: Rows include the study's own size and training-time sweeps, bias–variance measurements, and regularization comparisons. The paper also cites other studies' findings; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Values reported only graphically are not assigned numeric values.
record.test_reason: The study measures test loss against parameter count and training time for diffusion score models (DDPM U-Nets on CelebA, plus RFNN theory with simulations). It reports model-wise and epoch-wise double descent, bias–variance curves, multiple peaks and removal of the peak by regularization. This is a new setting (denoising score matching with m fixed noise realizations), not the original supervised-classification recipe, so it is T3 rather than T1. Parts also argue the shape needs restating (the post-peak plateau sits above the first minimum).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also stress that the test-loss rise sets in at p∼n independently of m, and that this rise and its bias mechanism persist even as the peak vanishes for m→∞. Since practice uses m≫1, observed overfitting is the rising branch toward a far-away peak. Optimally regularized large models (ridge or early stopping) beat unregularized models of any size.
record.recipe_differences: Uses parameter-count sweeps and test loss, but studies diffusion DSM with frozen noise realizations, RFNN theory and CelebA U-Nets rather than the original supervised-learning settings; also examines training time, bias–variance, and regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome and peak location vary with the number m of fixed noise realizations, sample count n, model width, diffusion time, and regularization/training time. For epoch-wise curves, the second descent occurs in the larger-width models and is sharper at larger width.

fits_no_version.finding: The test-loss rise begins at p∼n regardless of m, driven by growing bias as the model approaches the empirical (memorizing) score. Empirical test loss L_emp decreases benignly while the population test loss does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In denoising score matching, the implicit regularization behind benign overfitting targets the empirical score, making overparameterized overfitting malign: test loss plateaus above its earlier minimum.

record.problems: Empirical validation is restricted to one dataset, moderate sample counts, and models substantially smaller than state-of-the-art models. The study itself notes that U-Net feature learning and effective degrees of freedom may differ from RFNN scaling. Some results are shown in figures without numeric values in the text; the paper reports error bars for several experiments but not all.

untested.parts: Supervised classification and label-noise settings; only one dataset (CelebA 32×32 grayscale) and moderate n are tested.
Whether the late second descent persists. The authors cite prior work that sufficiently expressive diffusion models eventually turn back toward memorization, but they do not show this within τmax=2M.
Sample-wise non-monotonicity at fixed model size is not measured.
Fig. 8 left shows width and training time as substitutable axes. The authors say they give no insight into a single complexity measure, and none is validated.
No label-noise manipulation; no direct test that the peak is caused by noise.
No replotting against an effective parameter count. The weight-sharing remark is speculative.

missing.what: FID of early-stopped U-Nets vs p still shows double descent; test-loss and FID early-stopping criteria disagree
missing.locator: Section 3; Fig. 6 right (red); Appendix B.8, Fig. 13

missing.what: Large-p test-loss plateau grows as diffusion time t decreases (∝1/t for RFNN), for RFNN and U-Net W=128
Time-integrated U-Net test loss shows the same peak and above-minimum plateau
Fully-connected tanh network on a Gaussian mixture reproduces the peak near p≈nmd and the bias/variance pattern
Width–time coupling: the double descent in W emerges only at large τ, and its peak moves to smaller W as τ grows
At large t, RFNN overfitting is benign and zero regularization is optimal; at small t with m>1, the unregularized optimum is underparameterized

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The reader's V2 'challenges' label was removed: the small-model monotone curve matches the original's own regime structure, and the authors say so. In this paper m means noise realizations per sample, not label noise. The RFNN results are mainly analytical (replica method, Gaussian equivalence), checked against finite-d simulations. Preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-wise test-loss curves in RFNNs and U-Nets trained on diffusion objectives; it does not test the original supervised-learning settings.
Training-time curves are tested for U-Nets on CelebA, not across the original supervised-learning settings.
The study varies sample count and reports that the interpolation peak shifts with n, but does not establish that increasing training samples raises test error near that peak.
The study tests RFNNs and diffusion U-Nets, not a broad range of non-diffusion model classes.

The study notes that size and training time can act as substitutable axes in some curves, but does not propose or validate one effective-complexity measure that predicts peak location across size, epochs, and samples.

The study measures variance contributions, noise-realization count, multiple peaks, and regularization. It does not manipulate label noise specifically or establish that label noise causes the peak; the additional peak is not shown to be a triple-descent curve.

The study notes that convolutional weight sharing can decouple parameter count from effective degrees of freedom, but does not replot the second descent against an appropriate effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-curve.
